title: the Bhagavata's tenth book continued
hook: with Kamsa gone, Krishna goes to school, and the teacher's fee is a boy the ocean took
carry: going as far as it takes

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the Gita Govinda at its front door: bhakti as smarana, remembering, again and again, and your line, let the beloved come back to mind. Who came back to mind at the red light? Day nine hundred eighty-one.

Kamsa is dead. His father Ugrasena is back on the throne of Mathura. Vasudeva and Devaki have their sons again. So what does the hero of the story do next? He goes to school. The Bhagavata's tenth book picks up the thread here, right after the arena, and sends Krishna and his brother Balarama off to study with a teacher in the city of Avanti, a brahmin named Sandipani. They sit at his feet like any other students. And at the end, when it's time to pay, the teacher asks for something no student could give.
screen: `KAMSA IS GONE.` → `THE HERO GOES TO SCHOOL.` → `A FEE NO STUDENT COULD PAY.`

segments.voice: First, the strangeness of it. In the Bhagavata, Krishna is the Lord himself. Why would he need a teacher? The text's own answer, in paraphrase, is that the two brothers, though they were the source of all knowledge, chose to live in a teacher's house to show the world how it's done. They serve Sandipani, and they learn fast: the Vedas, the sciences, the use of weapons, the arts. Then comes the fee, the guru dakshina, the gift a student gives a teacher when the studies end. Sandipani talks it over with his wife. And they ask for the one thing they can't stop grieving: their son, who was lost in the ocean at Prabhasa. Not gold. Their boy. So Krishna and Balarama go to the shore. The ocean tells them a demon living in the shape of a conch, Panchajana, took the child. Krishna goes into the water, overcomes him, and takes the conch shell. The boy isn't there. So Krishna goes all the way to the city of Yama, the lord of death, and blows that conch at the gate. Yama comes out, honors him, and gives the child back. And the brothers walk home and hand their teacher his son. Two things are worth keeping. One is the order of loyalties. Before anything else in his new life, Krishna honors a teacher. The other is the size of the gift. A guru dakshina, in this story, isn't a payment that settles the account. It's the student going as far as it takes. And that conch, Panchajanya, doesn't leave the story. On the battlefield at the start of the Gita, it's the conch Krishna blows.
screen: `WHY WOULD THE LORD NEED A TEACHER?` · `THE FEE: OUR LOST SON.` · `A CONCH AT YAMA'S GATE.` · `THE STUDENT GOES AS FAR AS IT TAKES.` · then, large: `GURU DAKSHINA.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one teacher who changed something for you. A schoolteacher, a grandparent, a coach, someone at work. Picture the room where they taught you, and one thing they said there. Then ask, quietly: what would I give them, if I could? Don't worry about whether it's possible. Just let the answer come. If you pray, you can hold that teacher in your prayer. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with thanks. The bell holds the time.
Guru dakshina. The gift a student gives a teacher when the studies end. Today, Krishna as a student, and a teacher's fee paid at the gate of death.
Your line: going as far as it takes. Today, thank one teacher, out loud or in a short note, for one specific thing. Day nine hundred eighty-one.

screen: `DAY 981 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BHAGAVATA'S TENTH BOOK CONTINUED.`

howItsDone: Hindus honor teachers on Guru Purnima, and the custom of guru dakshina, a gift to a teacher at the end of study, continues in some traditional music, dance and scriptural schools; Krishna's fee to Sandipani is one story told when people speak of what a student owes a teacher.

trapdoor: what you thought: after defeating Kamsa, Krishna goes straight on to rule.
what it means: he goes to school with Sandipani, and pays his fee by bringing the teacher's dead son back from Yama.
what a scholar hears: the conch Panchajanya, won on this errand, is the one Krishna blows at the start of the Gita.
